A2.text:
Tural is twenty-seven. On Friday, he met his girlfriend Nigar's parents for the first time. He was very nervous.

“My father is very strict about manners,” Nigar told him. “Be polite, and please mind your manners.”

At dinner, Tural tried hard. He made small talk about the weather and the traffic. But then his phone rang. He answered it at the table. Nigar's father looked at him. That was rude.

Later, Nigar's father was telling a long story about his work. Tural wanted to say something funny, so he started to interrupt. Nigar kicked his foot under the table. “Bite your tongue,” she whispered.

After dinner, they went to the living room. There was a big, strange painting on the wall.

“What an ugly painting,” Tural laughed. “Who painted that?”

The room was quiet. “I did,” said Nigar's father.

Tural wanted to disappear. He did not want to offend anyone. He made an apology. “I'm very sorry. I don't understand art.”

Nigar's father looked at him for a long time. Then he started to laugh.

“You are the first honest person in this house,” he said. “Everybody says it is beautiful. I know it is terrible!”

Tural still had a lot to learn about respect and manners. But Nigar's father liked him.

B1.text:
Tural had been dating Nigar for a year when she finally invited him to dinner with her parents. On the metro, she gave him a list of rules. “My father is a retired school director. He cares about manners more than anything. Be polite, don't interrupt, and please — mind your manners.”

For the first hour, Tural did well. He brought flowers for her mother, stood up when her father entered the room and made polite small talk about the new metro station and the price of tomatoes. Then his phone rang. Without thinking, he answered it and spent two minutes discussing a football match with his brother. When he hung up, Nigar's father was watching him over his glasses. Tural could see he had rubbed him up the wrong way.

Things got worse during dessert. Her father was describing, in great detail, his first year as a teacher in Lankaran. Tural thought of a funny story of his own and opened his mouth to interrupt. Under the table, Nigar pressed his foot hard. “Bite your tongue,” she whispered through a smile.

Afterwards, they moved to the living room for tea. On the wall hung a large painting of what seemed to be a green horse eating the moon.

“Wow,” said Tural, trying to be relaxed. “Somebody really didn't know how to paint horses.”

The silence that followed was terrible.

“I painted that,” said Nigar's father quietly.

Tural felt his face burn. He hadn't meant to offend anyone. “I'm so sorry,” he said. “That was rude of me. Please accept my apology — I know nothing about art.”

Her father studied him for a long moment. Then, to everyone's surprise, he began to laugh until tears ran down his cheeks.

“Thirty years,” he said, wiping his eyes. “Thirty years of guests telling me it's a masterpiece. Finally, someone with the respect to tell me the truth.”

Nigar's mother poured more tea. Tural decided not to answer his phone for the rest of the year.

B2.text:
Tural and Nigar had been together for a year before she judged him ready to meet her parents. On the metro to their flat in Narimanov, she briefed him like a diplomat before a summit. “My father was a school director for thirty years. He judges people by their manners. Be polite, don't interrupt him, and for heaven's sake, mind your manners.”

The first hour went remarkably well. Tural presented flowers to her mother and a box of pakhlava for the table, rose to his feet when her father came in, and sustained twenty minutes of polite small talk about road works and the price of tomatoes. Then his phone rang, and on autopilot he answered it, discussing last night's derby with his brother for a full two minutes. When he looked up, Nigar's father was regarding him over the top of his glasses with an expression Tural recognised from his own school days. It is remarkably easy, he reflected, to rub someone up the wrong way in two minutes.

Dessert brought fresh danger. Her father was recounting, at considerable length, his first year teaching in a village near Lankaran. An anecdote of his own began to form in Tural's mind, and he drew breath to interrupt. Beneath the table, Nigar's heel came down on his toes. “Bite your tongue,” she murmured, without losing her smile.

Afterwards, they withdrew to the living room for tea. Above the sofa hung a large canvas depicting what appeared to be a green horse devouring the moon.

“Well,” said Tural, aiming for relaxed sophistication, “somebody clearly never saw a real horse.”

The silence that followed had texture.

“I painted it,” said Nigar's father evenly.

Tural felt the blood rush to his face. Offending his host had been the one thing he had sworn to avoid. “That was unforgivably rude,” he said. “I offer you my sincere apology. I'm afraid I know absolutely nothing about art.”

Her father considered him at length. Then, to universal astonishment, he threw back his head and laughed until he had to remove his glasses.

“Thirty years,” he gasped. “Thirty years of guests calling it a masterpiece. At last, a young man with enough respect for me to tell the truth.”

Nigar's mother refilled the glasses. Tural silently resolved to switch off his phone for the remainder of the decade.

podcast.title: Sorry, I mean thank you

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Are you a polite person? Guess: what does Sam say when someone steps on his foot?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is manners. And I have to say sorry first.
Sorry for what?
Nothing! That's the problem. British people say sorry all the time. Someone steps on my foot, and I say sorry.
[laugh] That's too polite, Sam.
I know. What surprised me in Baku was the respect for older people.
Yes. On the bus, young people always stand up for an older person. Not doing it is really rude.
And at Mr Aliyev's house, I learned you never say no to tea.
Never! Tea is the first thing a guest gets. Saying no is almost an insult.
Then there is small talk. Here a taxi driver asked me how much I earn — in the first minute!
[chuckle] What did you say?
In England we say: bite your tongue. So I just smiled and talked about the weather.
In my family, people interrupt each other all the time. It's not rude — it means we're interested.
At my first dinner with your family, I waited for a pause. There was no pause! [laugh]
My grandmother is strict about one thing: the table. When Aysu takes food before the guests, she says, "Mind your manners!"
My mum said exactly the same to me. In English!
So what's the most important rule for you?
A real apology. Not my automatic "sorry" — a real one, when you are wrong.
I agree. And showing respect to everyone, from the cleaner to the boss.
Well said. Sorry, I mean — thank you. [chuckle]
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what is polite in your country but rude somewhere else?
Tell us — and don't interrupt your partner! See you next time!
Bye for now!
